title: Finishing a tractate
hookLine: a celebration when a tractate is completed
last: AN ARGUMENT FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE ENDURES.

lines: A BOOK CLOSES. A PARTY STARTS.
cards: The last line of a tractate. Someone reads it aloud, slowly, and the room that has been quiet for an hour suddenly isn't. A cake appears from somewhere.

Someone pours a drink. Someone else stands up to say a few words about the final page, gets interrupted, and starts again. Months of study, sometimes years, one page at a time, and now the book is closed.
It is not a quiet moment. It's a party. Today's word is the name of that party.

teach.b: Siyum. Completion, and the celebration that marks it. First, an old feast.
The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, tells of the sage Abaye saying that whenever he saw a young scholar finish a tractate, he made a feast for the rabbis. Notice whose finish it was. Not his own.
He threw the party for somebody else's last page. Second, what's said. At a siyum, those who finished say a short traditional text called the hadran.

It speaks to the tractate itself, by name, as if to a friend: we will return to you, and you will return to us. We won't forget you, and you won't forget us. The ending isn't goodbye; it's see you again.

teach.h: A MEAL THAT IS A COMMANDMENT.
teach.b: The meal after a siyum is treated as a seudat mitzvah, a meal that is itself part of a commandment, like the meal at a wedding or a circumcision. A custom grows out of that.
On the day before Passover, by custom, firstborns fast. Some attend a siyum that morning, and joining its meal releases them from the fast. Fourth, the size.

teach.h: A KITCHEN TABLE OR A GREAT HALL.
teach.b: A siyum can be three people around a kitchen table who finished a small tractate together, or a crowd in a large hall when a daily study cycle reaches the end of the whole Talmud.
Same words, same promise to return.

how: When a person or group completes a tractate, they hold a siyum: the last passage is read, the hadran is recited, someone teaches a few words on the tractate, and a festive meal follows. A siyum is often held on the morning before Passover so that firstborns may join the meal.

games.q: you've just read the last line of a tractate you've studied for months. the room goes quiet. what do you say to the book?
o: we will return to you, and you will return to us.
nothing; open the next one at once.
games.why: the hadran speaks to the tractate by name and promises to come back. a siyum isn't goodbye; it's see you again.

practice: Bring to mind something you finished recently, a project, a book, a hard week, a course of treatment, and let yourself see its last page. Don't judge how well it went; a siyum marks reaching the end, not doing it perfectly.
Then tell it, quietly, what the hadran tells a tractate: I'll come back to you.

wordCard.voice: Siyum. Completion: the celebration when a tractate, or another unit of study, is finished, with the hadran's promise to return. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: completion; the celebration when a unit of study is finished.
